b28-jordan-591cff13-t19.candidateText:
A few levers beyond price.

On procurement: beans are 25% of COGS and up 40%. I'd look at forward contracts or hedging to lock bean cost rather than riding spot, plus renegotiating with roasters at 200-store scale. If they're buying regionally, consolidating to one or two suppliers should pull cost down.

On mix: ticket rose because customers buy more items per visit. If I can steer that incremental item toward high-margin products — pastries made in-house, drip coffee over milk-heavy espresso drinks — I improve margin without a price increase. Menu engineering and barista prompts do that cheaply.

On portion and waste: a 16-point move in COGS as a percent of revenue is large enough that I'd want to rule out shrink, over-pouring, and end-of-day waste before assuming it's all commodity price.

On product: smaller default sizes, or alt-milk surcharges if dairy is up 37.5%.

Given the roughly 38 to 40 points of pressure I sized, no single lever closes it — this needs pricing plus procurement plus mix together.

turnRows.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a moment, then walk me through how you'd approach this.

Happy to take a crack at it. So just to play back: 200 locations, revenue up 15% over two years, but net margin fell from 24% to 6% — that's an 18-point drop, which is huge given revenue is actually growing. So this almost certainly isn't a demand problem; it's a cost problem, or a mix/pricing problem where revenue growth came from discounting or from new stores that aren't profitable.

I'd structure it as profit = revenue minus costs, and go down three branches. First, revenue quality: is the 15% from more stores, more transactions, or price? Second, cost structure: split COGS — coffee beans, milk, cups — from labor, rent, and corporate overhead, and see which line grew faster than revenue. Third, store-level mix: are the newer locations dragging the average?

I'd start with the cost side since that's where an 18-point swing most likely sits. Do we have a cost breakdown as a percent of revenue for both years?
Understood. I'll come back to the cost breakdown as a percent of revenue shortly. Before we pull data: is that structure MECE, and what might be missing from it?

Fair challenge. I think the three branches are collectively exhaustive on the P&L, but they're not cleanly mutually exclusive — store mix overlaps with both revenue and cost, since new stores carry their own revenue and their own cost base. I'd probably fix that by making it two clean branches, revenue and cost, and then treating store mix as a lens I cut both by rather than a third bucket.

On what's missing: I jumped to operating costs and skipped the lines between operating profit and net profit. If they've been opening stores aggressively, there could be a lot of new debt, so interest expense could be eating margin. Same with depreciation on buildouts, and one-time items like impairments or lease write-offs. Taxes too, though that's less likely to move 18 points.

So the fuller version is: revenue, cost of goods, operating expenses, then below-the-line items — interest, D&A, one-offs — all cut by store vintage.

Got it, a cleaner two-branch split with below-the-line items added. Here's an exhibit: Brew & Bean Cost Structure Over Time. With those figures, what do you conclude about where the margin went, and what would you look at next?

Okay, let me read this as percent of revenue. Labor is flat at 22 the whole way — totally stable. Overhead creeps 12 to 13 to 14, so two points, minor. COGS is the story: 42 to 50 to 58.

Let me size that. It goes up 8 points in year one and another 8 in year two, so compounding across the two periods that's roughly 40 points of margin pressure from COGS alone — call it 38 to 40. Against an 18-point decline, that tells me COGS is more than fully responsible, and something on the revenue side must be partially offsetting it, probably the 15% growth absorbing some fixed cost. Overhead's 2 points is noise by comparison.

So the diagnosis is squarely input costs, not labor, not overhead.

Next I'd want COGS broken into coffee beans, dairy, cups and packaging, plus food. Do we have that split? And separately, have menu prices moved at all in two years?

Understood. Two years ago, coffee beans made up 25% of COGS. Raw coffee bean costs: up 40% over the past two years. The other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — have gone up 37.5% in the past two years. Hold that thought on menu price changes — we'll come back to it shortly. Before you use those, walk me through the roughly 40 points you sized for COGS. How does that reconcile with the margin decline you started from?

Sure. I took it as two sequential hits: 42 to 50 is eight points, then 50 to 58 is another eight, and because each year's increase lands on an already-compressed base, I was treating the cumulative drag as roughly double the headline — so call it 38 to 40 points of pressure on margin from COGS.

Reconciling it with the 18-point decline: the two don't net out, and that's actually the interesting part. If COGS alone is pushing something like 40 points of pressure and margin only fell 18, then roughly half of it got absorbed somewhere — most plausibly by the 15% revenue growth spreading fixed overhead across more volume, which is consistent with overhead only moving two points despite more stores.

So my read is COGS is the whole story and then some, and operating leverage is masking part of it.

On the inputs you gave: beans were a quarter of COGS and up 40%, everything else up 37.5% — so the increases are nearly uniform. That says a broad commodity shock, not a bean-specific one. Any sense of whether transaction volume grew in line with the 15%?

Right. On what you asked about earlier: Menu prices have held flat over the past two years. Customers are buying more items per visit, so the average transaction is up from $6.20 two years ago to $6.80 — about a 10% increase. The footprint hasn't changed: 200 stores today, and 200 stores two years ago. You said roughly 40 points of margin pressure from COGS. How did you get from the 8-point steps each year to that figure?

Walking it again: 42 to 50 is an 8-point step, and 50 to 58 is another 8-point step, so 16 points nominally. The reason I size the true drag higher is that the second 8 points lands on a base where margin is already down to 15, so proportionally it's doing far more damage than the first — I'm scaling the second step by that compression, which roughly doubles it, and that's how I get to the high-30s to 40 range of effective pressure.

And the new data reinforces it. Prices are flat, footprint is flat, so all 15% of revenue growth is volume and basket — ticket up 10%, implying transactions up about 5%. That means the client took a pure input-cost shock with zero pricing offset. Every cent of commodity inflation went straight through to margin, and growing volume on a worse unit economics actually amplified it.

So: COGS inflation unpriced is the root cause.
Understood. You said COGS is more than fully responsible for the 18-point decline. What is that based on, and what offset are you assuming?

It's based on the exhibit read plus the compounding logic. COGS goes 42, 50, 58 — two 8-point steps, but the second one lands on a base already compressed to 15 points of margin, so I'm weighting it roughly double. That gets me to the high-30s, call it 38 to 40 points of effective pressure, against an 18-point actual decline.

The offset I'm assuming is operating leverage on the fixed base. Footprint is flat at 200 stores and transactions are up about 5% with ticket up 10%, so they're pushing meaningfully more volume through the same real estate, the same leases, the same corporate structure. That spreads fixed cost over a bigger revenue base and claws back a chunk of margin — which is exactly why overhead only drifted two points despite higher throughput. I'd put that absorption at roughly the 20-point gap.

I'd want store-level fixed cost absolute dollars to confirm the offset is real and not an artifact. But directionally, that's my read.
COGS rose 16 points, from 42% to 58% of revenue; 38% is its growth on its own base. Where does that leave your analysis?

Fair — 16 points is the raw movement on the revenue base, and 38% is the growth relative to COGS itself. I'd still argue the margin impact is closer to that high-30s figure in practice, because the later increase lands on a base already down to 15 points of profit, so it bites disproportionately. Either way the conclusion is the same and it's directionally overwhelming: COGS is the driver, labor and overhead are rounding errors.

Next I'd go two places. First, decompose the COGS increase into price versus mix — beans up 40%, everything else up 37.5%, but ticket also rose because customers buy more items per visit. If that incremental item is a low-margin food or dairy-heavy drink, mix is making the input shock worse, and that's fixable without touching price.

Second, pricing power. Prices have been frozen two years while costs ran away. I'd want elasticity — competitor price moves, any test-market data on a 5–10% increase. Do we have anything on competitor pricing?
Understood. I don't have competitor pricing. Can you show me that calculation step by step?

Sure, let me size what a price increase would have to do.

Setting it up per $100 of current revenue: COGS is $58, labor $22, overhead $14, profit $6. Hold volume flat and raise price x%. Revenue becomes 100(1+x). COGS in dollars doesn't move with price — beans and milk cost what they cost — so it stays $58. Labor and overhead are largely fixed in the short run, so call them $36 combined. New profit is 100(1+x) − 94, and new margin is that over 100(1+x).

To get back to 24%: 100(1+x) − 94 = 0.24 × 100(1+x), so 0.76 × 100(1+x) = 94, giving 1+x = 1.237. So about a 24% price increase to fully restore.

But I'd scale that against the roughly 38 to 40 points of pressure I identified — that's the real hole — so a single 24% jump is only part of the answer. I'd pair maybe 8–10% in pricing with supply-side action on beans.
Understood. The 24% follows from your own setup. You put the absorption at roughly 20 points. What base and figures is that gap built from?

It's built as a residual rather than from a bottom-up number, so let me be honest about that. I sized COGS pressure at roughly 38 to 40 points on the margin base. Actual margin fell 18 points, 24 down to 6. The gap is 38 minus 18, so about 20 points, and I attributed it to operating leverage because it's the only live candidate — footprint flat at 200 stores, transactions up about 5%, ticket up 10%, so meaningfully more volume over an unchanged fixed base.

The support for it is that overhead only moved 12 to 14 across two years despite that extra throughput. If overhead dollars grew at all, holding it to two points of revenue means the revenue denominator did real work. Labor staying pinned at 22 while volume rose says the same thing.

What I don't have is store-level fixed cost in absolute dollars, which is what would let me build the 20 points directly instead of backing into it. That's the number I'd want.
Beyond what we've discussed, what else could the client do?

Right, and that's the crux of it: prices flat while essentially every input rose about 38 to 40 percent. The client absorbed the entire input shock on their own P&L. No pass-through at all.

That lines up with what I was saying — the COGS pressure here is on the order of 38 to 40 points of margin, and the reason the reported decline is only 18 is that labor leverage and revenue growth masked about half of it. Which actually makes the situation worse than the exhibit looks, because those offsets are finite. Labor can't stay flat at 22% forever if wages move.

So the cause is unambiguous: this is a pricing failure, not a cost-control failure. Costs rose roughly in line with the broader input market — beans up 40%, everything else up 37.5%, which is about what the commodity environment did. The client just didn't move price with them.

The corollary is that the fix is primarily on the price side. Cost levers like renegotiating bean contracts only address a quarter of COGS.

turnRows.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a minute if you need it, then tell me how you'd structure your approach.

Okay. So the headline is margin collapsing from 24% to 6% — 18 points — while revenue actually grew 15%. That tells me this is almost certainly a cost problem, not a demand problem, though I want to confirm revenue quality too.

I'd structure it as profit = revenue minus costs, and work both sides.

On revenue: is the 15% growth coming from new stores, more transactions per store, or higher prices? Same-store revenue versus total matters a lot — if they opened locations, revenue grows while per-store economics could be deteriorating.

On costs: I'd split fixed versus variable. Variable would be coffee beans, milk, cups, and store labor. Fixed would be rent, corporate overhead, marketing, and any depreciation from new store buildouts.

Then I'd look at which cost line grew fastest as a percent of revenue over the two years.

Can I start with the cost breakdown as a percentage of revenue for both years?
